title: USDA soil orders

definition.text: The twelve top-level classes of USDA soil taxonomy, whose criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed.

facts.text: Order names end in -sol: Alfisols, Andisols, Aridisols, Entisols, Gelisols, Histosols, Inceptisols, Mollisols, Oxisols, Spodosols, Ultisols and Vertisols.
Each order reflects distinct soil-forming processes and characteristics such as climate, vegetation and mineral composition.
In order of increasing development they run Entisols, Inceptisols, Aridisols, Mollisols, Alfisols, Spodosols, Ultisols and Oxisols; Histosols and Vertisols can appear at any stage.
Many orders hinge on diagnostic horizons: Alfisols and Ultisols need an argillic or kandic horizon, Mollisols a mollic epipedon, Oxisols an oxic horizon and Spodosols a spodic horizon.
By share of global ice-free land, Entisols lead with 16.3%, then Aridisols (12.7%), Inceptisols (9.9%) and Alfisols (9.6%); Andisols are smallest at 0.7%.
In the United States, Mollisols cover the most ice-free land (22.4%), followed by Alfisols (14.5%), while Oxisols cover less than 0.01%.
Mountain soils, a mixture of orders or soil-free 'Rugged Mountains', make up the remaining 11.6% of ice-free land.
The 1975 taxonomy recognized 10 orders; the 1999 second edition recognized 12.

notes: Section of USDA soil taxonomy (a classification-systems seed), drafted here as this chapter's overview. The order list in USDA soil taxonomy#Discussion gives rounder worldwide shares that differ for some orders; see the conflicts on Entisol, Inceptisol and Spodosol.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of moderately leached soils with a clay-enriched subsoil and relatively high native fertility.

facts.text: They form in semi-arid to humid areas, typically under hardwood forest, and must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon.
The name comes from 'alf', for aluminium (Al) and iron (Fe), a root inherited from the old pedalfer group.
By definition they have at least 35% base saturation, so calcium, magnesium and potassium are relatively abundant; the more leached Ultisols fall below 35%.

Productive and abundant, they are among the most important orders for food and fibre, though Australian and African Alfisols lack nitrogen and phosphorus and monsoonal ones acidify under heavy cultivation.
They cover about one-tenth of the ice-free land (9.6% globally, 14.5% of the U.S.) and dominate areas such as the Ohio River basin, the Baltic region and Sudan.
In eastern North America, Alfisols occur in glaciated areas, while Ultisols lie south of the limit of maximum glaciation.
Suborders follow wetness and climate: oxygen-depleted Aqualfs, cold Cryalfs, humid Udalfs, semiarid Ustalfs and Mediterranean Xeralfs.
In the WRB most Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols, some Retisols or Nitisols; Aqualfs are mainly Stagnosols or Planosols, and natric Alfisols Solonetz.

definition.text: The record of Alfisol paleosols, which reaches back to woodland and early forest soils of the Late Devonian.

facts.text: Probably owing to their fertility, Alfisols are the oldest forest soils; the oldest lie in the Aztec Siltstone of Victoria Land, Antarctica, with fossil wood and spores of Archaeopteris-Callixylon trees.
Large woody roots pipe water and clay downward and leave material in the subsoil as they decay, the likely reason argillic horizons, Alfisols and forests go together.
All tetrapod bones and tracks from Late Devonian and Mississippian paleosols of New York and Pennsylvania occur in Aridisols and Alfisols.
Trace fossils such as the nest cells of ground-nesting bees (Celliforma) and termite nests also occur in Alfisols, as well as in Aridisols and Oxisols.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils formed in volcanic ash, rich in glass and in amorphous colloids such as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite.

facts.text: They must have andic properties: abundant poorly crystalline iron and aluminium minerals, high phosphorus, low bulk density and high organic matter.
Being generally young, they are usually very fertile, except where phosphorus is easily fixed, as sometimes happens in the tropics.

They support intensive use: wet rice on Java feeds some of the world's densest populations, others grow fruit, maize, tea, coffee or tobacco, and Pacific Northwest Andisols carry very productive forests.
They cover about 1% of global ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand's North Island.
Suborders are wet Aquands, very cold Gelands, very dry Torrands, semiarid Ustands, dry-summer Xerands and young, glassy, coarse Vitrands.
In the WRB they are known as Andosols, though some WRB Histosols are Andisols and some Andosols are Inceptisols.
Fossil Andisols occur far from present-day volcanoes, some dated to the Mesoproterozoic, 1.5 billion years ago.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of dry soils of arid and semi-arid climates, also called desert soils.

facts.text: Water deficiency is the defining trait: they have an aridic moisture regime, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and are not leached.
They also need enough age to show subsoil weathering, including some diagnostic subsurface horizon; an ochric epipedon is common.
Named from Latin aridus, 'dry', they dominate deserts and xeric shrublands, about one-third of Earth's land surface, and cover 12.7% of global ice-free land.
Sparse vegetation leaves them very low in organic matter, and soil formation is slow.
Limited leaching leaves subsurface horizons of deposited clay, sodium, calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts, sometimes cemented, as in caliche or duripans.
Many have well-developed Bt horizons from clay moved in past wetter periods, and salt build-up at the surface can cause salinization.
In the WRB most Aridisols are Calcisols, Gypsisols, Durisols or Solonchaks.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils with no profile development beyond an A horizon and no diagnostic horizons, little changed from their parent material.

facts.text: They are the most common order, covering about 16% of global ice-free land (16.3% in the order table) and 12.2% of the U.S.
Development is held back by unweatherable parent material, erosion, repeated deposition by floods, wind or slope processes, shallow bedrock, or toxic materials such as serpentine or mine spoil.
They are common on river and beach sediments and volcanic ash, and some are just an A horizon on bedrock.
Suborders are Aquents, saturated soils of riverbanks and mudflats; Fluvents, alluvium renewed by floods; shallow Orthents; sandy Psamments; and Wassents, under water over 21 hours a day.
So varied are they that their suborders match different WRB groups: Psamments Arenosols, Fluvents Fluvisols, many Orthents Regosols or Leptosols, Wassents Gleysols.
In Australia most Entisols are called Rudosols or Tenosols.
Most fossil soils from before land plants spread in the Silurian are Entisols, but unlike other orders they reveal little about past climate.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy says Entisols are 18% of soils worldwide.
conflicts.note: Same measure (share of ice-free land, S:0da82a5078bb); the order table gives 16.3% (S:4fe0f587ba75) and the Entisol page about 16% (S:022a0f35abfe).

title: Orthent

definition.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols that lack horizon development because of steep slopes or parent materials with no lasting weatherable minerals.

facts.text: Typically exceedingly shallow, they are also called skeletal soils, or lithosols in the FAO classification; any former soil has been removed or truncated.
Most lie on very steep mountain slopes, where erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form; in Australia and parts of Africa they occur on flat land whose rock has no weatherable minerals.
Shallow, steep and erosion-prone, they are unfit for arable farming and carry only low stocking rates, but are important wildlife habitat.
Many belong to WRB Regosols or Leptosols, and they can mark extremely ancient landscapes with minimal soil formation, as in Australia today.

notes: Assigned to classification-systems by the dossier; drafted here next to Entisol and Psamment.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of very cold climates, defined by permafrost within two metres of the surface.

facts.text: The order table requires permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm.
The name comes from Latin gelare, 'to freeze', after the cryoturbation caused by alternate freezing and thawing.
Organic matter builds up on top, so most are black or dark brown over a shallow mineral layer; calcium and potassium leach easily above the permafrost, limiting fertility.
Permafrost greatly restricts engineering use, as large structures subside when the frozen ground thaws.
They lie chiefly in Siberia, Alaska and Canada, with smaller areas in the Andes, Tibet, northern Scandinavia and ice-free Greenland and Antarctica, covering 8.6% of global ice-free land.
Slow decomposition makes them an important sink for carbon dioxide.
Gelisols key out before Histosols in soil taxonomy, so organic permafrost soils are Histels there but Cryic Histosols in the WRB, where most Gelisols are Cryosols.
Fossil Gelisols are known from Precambrian ice ages 900 million years ago.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy defines Gelisols by permafrost within two metres, or gelic materials and permafrost within one metre.
conflicts.note: The order table (S:1aed59a2ba65) puts the depths the other way round: permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm; the Gelisol page (S:1c6d2a9e2aed) gives permafrost within two metres.

definition.text: The three suborders of Gelisols: organic Histels, frost-churned Turbels and little-churned Orthels.

facts.text: Histels resemble Histosols but have permafrost within two metres and 80% or more organic material in the top 50 cm; they dominate subarctic and low-arctic permafrost regions.
Turbels show cryoturbation through more than a third of the active layer, with broken horizons, involutions, patterned ground and ice or sand wedges; they lie mainly in continuous permafrost.
Orthels show little cryoturbation, affecting less than a third of the active layer, and occur mainly in discontinuous permafrost and alpine areas.
Cryoturbation is much stronger on exposed sites, where Turbels dominate, than in sheltered valleys.

definition.text: A soil, in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy, made primarily of organic materials.

facts.text: It has 40 cm or more of organic soil material starting within 40 cm of the surface; organic material means at least 12% organic carbon in Soil Taxonomy or 20% in the WRB.
Its materials are muck (sapric), mucky peat (hemic) or peat (fibric), and Soil Taxonomy's suborders Saprists, Hemists and Fibrists follow them, alongside drier Folists and submerged Wassists.
Histosols form wherever organic matter accumulates faster than it is destroyed, usually because poor drainage prevents aerobic decay; with enough time, coal forms.
With Gelisols they store large quantities of organic carbon, which makes them ecologically very important.
They have very low bulk density, and many are acidic and short of major nutrients, especially rain-fed raised bogs cut off from groundwater.
Hard to cultivate, drained Histosols on young glacial land can make good dairy or beef pasture, but dried organic matter can blow away as powder and heavy structures subside.
Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea; they cover 1.2% of global ice-free land.
Known as peat or muck in many countries and as Organosols in Australia, they appear as fossils with the first extensive land vegetation in the Devonian.

title: Spodosol

definition.text: A USDA soil order of acid soils with a spodic horizon, where organic matter complexed with iron and aluminium has accumulated after leaching from the layer above.

facts.text: They must have a spodic horizon within 2 m of the surface and lack andic properties; most also have a bleached albic horizon.
Their B horizon holds illuviated aluminium with organic matter, and often iron.
Typical of coniferous and boreal forests in cool, moist climates such as southeastern Alaska and the Great Lakes, they are also Florida's most prominent order.
They cover 2.6% of global and 3.3% of U.S. ice-free land.
They correspond to the Podzols of Russia and northern and central Europe and to Canada's Podzolic soils; Australia calls them Podosols.
Spodosols are known only from the Carboniferous onward, though less acidic look-alikes from the Mesozoic and Tertiary may be an extinct suborder.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy says Spodosols are 4% of soils worldwide.
conflicts.note: Same measure (share of ice-free land, S:0da82a5078bb); the order table gives 2.6% (S:0f66a8f2e0a2).

notes: No Spodosol article was crawled (it redirects to Podzol, a world-reference-base-soil-groups seed); drafted with no article so the twelve orders are complete. Passes the 2+ pages test (USDA soil taxonomy, Soil in the United States, Paleopedological record, Podzol). Overlaps the Podzol entry.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of young soils with little to moderate development and weathering, more developed than Entisols.

facts.text: A B horizon has begun to form, but there is no diagnostic subsurface horizon of another order; soils that fit no other order may default to Inceptisols.
Profiles vary widely but usually have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon; some have histic or plaggen epipedons, calcic horizons, duripans or fragipans.
They occur everywhere except extremes such as deserts and permafrost: on mountains, sand dunes, fresh coastal and river deposits and late Pleistocene glacial drift.
They develop on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have supported more developed Alfisols.
Suborders follow temperature, moisture, saturation and epipedon: wet Aquepts, human-made Anthrepts, cold Gelepts and Cryepts, humid Udepts, semiarid Ustepts and dry-summer Xerepts.
Many crops grow on them, but Ustepts and Xerepts may need irrigation and Aquepts drainage, except those with a sulfuric horizon, where draining can produce sulfuric acid.
They cover 9.9% of global and 9.1% of U.S. ice-free land.

conflicts.text: The order list in USDA soil taxonomy says Inceptisols are 15% of soils worldwide.
conflicts.note: Same measure (share of ice-free land, S:0da82a5078bb); the order table gives 9.9% (S:77876d361769).

definition.text: A USDA soil order of soils with a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon.

facts.text: The mollic epipedon, typically 60 to 80 cm deep, builds up from long-term additions of organic matter from roots and usually has a soft, granular structure.
Mollisols must have base saturation above 50% and are common in grasslands.
They form in savannas and mountain valleys, as in Central Asia and the North American Great Plains, landscapes long shaped by fire and by ants and earthworms churning the soil.
As the world's most agriculturally productive order they are among the most economically important; a 2003 estimate found only 14 to 26 percent of grasslands still relatively natural.
They cover about 7% of global ice-free land but 22.4% of the United States, more than any other order there.
In the WRB, Mollisols split into Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems; shallow ones may be Leptosols, many Aquolls are Gleysols and natric ones Solonetz.
Soils with a mollic epipedon key out elsewhere when other traits dominate: as Vertisols where shrink–swell clays rule, as Andisols where andic properties take precedence.
Their development is tied to the cooling and drying of global climate in the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene; fossils are confidently known from the Eocene.

definition.text: The seven suborders of Mollisols, set mainly by soil moisture and temperature regimes.

facts.text: Albolls and Aquolls are wet soils with an aquic moisture regime; Albolls also have an eluvial horizon.
Cryolls have a frigid or cryic temperature regime, and Gelolls a mean annual soil temperature below 0 °C.
Udolls, Ustolls and Xerolls carry the udic, ustic and xeric moisture regimes of humid, subhumid and Mediterranean climates.
Mollisol-like permafrost soils of Tibet and the Andean altiplano, called Molliturbels or Mollorthels, are not acidic and make the best grazing land in those cold climates.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of very highly weathered soils rich in iron and aluminium oxides, best known from tropical rainforest within 25 degrees of the Equator.

facts.text: They show the most profile development of any order and must have an oxic horizon within 150 cm; at all depths they hold no more than 10% weatherable minerals and have low cation exchange capacity.
Iron(III) and aluminium oxides and hydroxides make them always red or yellowish, alongside quartz and kaolin; the name comes from 'oxide'.
Weathering, humification and mixing by animals form them; rain acidified by forest litter leaches the minerals, so plants depend on nutrients from decaying litter.
Low CEC and strong phosphorus fixation on iron and aluminium oxides make permanent cropping hard, but regions able to afford lime and fertilizer farm them intensively, as with Brazilian soybeans.
Today they occur almost only in tropical South America and Africa, mostly on stable cratons; they cover 7.6% of global ice-free land but under 0.01% of the U.S.
Suborders are wet Aquox, continuously humid Perox, humid Udox, semiarid Ustox and arid Torrox, which are always paleosols from wetter times, mainly in Southern Africa.
In the WRB they are mainly Ferralsols, some Plinthosols or Nitisols, and some were once classed as laterite soils.
Fossil Oxisols date from the first free oxygen in the atmosphere, about 2,200 million years ago, and in warm periods such as the Mesozoic they reached North America and Europe.

definition.text: A USDA soil order of strongly weathered, acid mineral soils, commonly known as red clay soils.

facts.text: They hold no calcareous material, under 10% weatherable minerals in the top layer and under 35% base saturation throughout, and must have an argillic or kandic horizon.
The name comes from 'ultimate': they were seen as the end product of continuous weathering in a humid climate without renewal by glaciation.
Iron oxide colours them from purplish-red to pale yellowish-orange; they are typically quite acidic, often below pH 5, and kaolinite is often the main clay.
Short of calcium and potassium, they need lime and fertilizer for settled farming and are more easily exhausted than Alfisols or Mollisols; organic-rich Humults are relatively fertile.
Kaolinite gives good bearing capacity and no shrink–swell, so well-drained Ultisols such as the Cecil series suit urban development.
They dominate the Southern United States, southeastern China and Southeast Asia, and cover 8.5% of global ice-free land.
Taking hundreds of thousands of years to form, they stop sharply at the limit of maximum Pleistocene glaciation in North America.
In the WRB most are Acrisols or Alisols, some Retisols or Nitisols; Acrisols match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders.

definition.text: Managing the low organic matter and low pH of red clay Ultisols so that garden plants can grow.

facts.text: Amendments are generally needed every year, guided by soil tests, and lime raises the typically low pH.
Gardeners aim for about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter and 50% pore space; North Carolina Ultisol is roughly 82% mineral, 2% organic matter and 16% pore space.
Mulch makes the soil more porous, and 2 to 3 inches of compost and manure mixed to a shovel's depth add organic matter, best in the fall so microbes release nutrients in time.
Some gardeners skip amending by using raised beds or Hügelkultur, or grow native plants adapted to damp, poorly drained soils.

title: Vertisol

definition.text: A soil rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet; an order in USDA soil taxonomy and a WRB Reference Soil Group.

facts.text: They need more than 30% clay to 50 cm and usually have a mollic epipedon; they form in clay-rich material, often from basic rocks such as basalt, in seasonally humid or erratic climates.
Alternate shrinking and swelling makes the soil plough itself (argillipedoturbation), giving some a very deep A horizon and no B horizon and heaving subsoil up as gilgai.
Colours range from grey or red to deep black: 'black earths' in Australia, 'black gumbo' in East Texas, 'black cotton' soils in East Africa.
Found between 50°N and 45°S, they dominate eastern Australia, India's Deccan Plateau, parts of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya and the lower Paraná, covering 2.4% of global ice-free land.
Natural vegetation is grassland, savanna or grassy woodland, because the heavy, unstable soil makes it hard for trees to grow.
Very hard when dry and sticky when wet, they are hard to farm without irrigation, but near-impermeability when saturated suits rice; most are grazed by cattle or sheep.
Shrink–swell damages buildings and roads but lets the soil recover quickly from compaction; Australians prize them as among the few soils not acutely short of phosphorus.
The WRB's diagnostic vertic horizon has at least 30% clay, shrink–swell cracks and wedge-shaped aggregates or slickensides; Australia calls these soils Vertosols.

notes: The USDA soil taxonomy order table (S:d1678cd14090) calls the deep cracks gilgai, while this page (S:84f410c781fa) uses gilgai for the heaved microrelief; see the pilot's Gilgai entry.

definition.text: The six USDA suborders of Vertisols, set by wetness, temperature and how long their cracks stay open.

facts.text: Aquerts have aquic conditions and redoximorphic features; slow permeability brings ponding, and reduced manganese may help darken the profile.
Cryerts, with a cryic regime, are most extensive in the Canadian Prairies; Xererts, with cracks open in summer and closed in winter, in the eastern Mediterranean and California.
Usterts, with cracks open at least 90 cumulative days a year, are the most extensive suborder worldwide, though Torrerts are the most extensive in Australia.
Uderts, with cracks open less than 90 days a year and sometimes only in droughts, are rare, mostly in Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

definition.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols made of unconsolidated sand, found in shifting dunes or in very coarse parent material weathered for millions of years.

facts.text: A Psamment has no distinct horizons and must be loamy sand or coarser all the way through.
Psamments cover 3.4% of the global land mass, abundant in the deserts of Africa and Australia, on old landforms of eastern South America and in Florida and Nebraska's Sand Hills.
Their poorly graded, constantly mixed sand gives them very low water-holding capacity.

Being highly siliceous, they are extremely low in nutrients, especially phosphorus, and highly acidic except in very arid climates; young glacial Psamments of northern Europe are somewhat more fertile.
Their vegetation is often remarkably well adapted, as in the species-rich Fynbos of South Africa's Cape and the Kwongan of Western Australia.
Few are farmed: fertilizing is costly, yields stay below other soils of the region, and the sand erodes very easily.
USDA soil taxonomy divides them by temperature and moisture regime into Cryopsamments, Torripsamments, Ustipsamments and Xeropsamments, plus Quartzipsamments with over 90 percent resistant minerals.
In the WRB most Psamments are Arenosols, but those of river, lake or marine origin are Fluvisols.

definition.text: Organic soil material, as in a Histosol, so thoroughly decomposed that plant parts and even faecal matter can no longer be identified.

facts.text: The WRB defines sapric material as having less than one-sixth of its volume as recognizable plant tissue within 100 cm; USDA soil taxonomy uses a fibre content below one-sixth.
Muck is sapric soil that is naturally waterlogged or artificially drained; the USDA NRCS definition requires saturation for more than 30 cumulative days in normal years.
Canada places muck soils in its Organic order, with at least 30% organic matter and a depth of at least 40 cm.
Sapric soils are deep, dark and friable, often underlain by marl or marly clay.

title: Muck farming

definition.text: Farming drained swamp soils of sapric organic matter, or muck, mostly for vegetables.

facts.text: Muck grows specialty crops such as onions, carrots, celery and potatoes, and matters to farming in New York, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin and Florida.

Torrey Farms' muckland at Elba, New York, is thought to be the world's largest continuous section; the Black Dirt Region's 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest U.S. concentration outside the Everglades.
Because draining wetlands destroys habitat, muck farming is controversial, and U.S. environmental regulations make new muckland unlikely.
The light soil needs windbreaks, can burn underground for months, and oxidizes away each year, growing shallower and releasing carbon dioxide.

notes: S:c13431620960 is flagged CONTESTED: the source calls muck farming controversial for its environmental cost but presents no opposing case, so it is not marked as a debate.

definition.text: The study of soils of past geological eras, from the recent Quaternary back to the earliest periods of Earth's history.

facts.text: It can be seen as a branch of soil science or of paleontology, since its methods combine the two.
It began with observations in Scotland around 1795 of cliff soils that seemed to be remains of a former land surface.
Interest grew once soils were tied to climate: Hilgard related them in the United States in 1892, and by the 1920s Glinka had found Russian soils that were relics of warmer climates.
Fossil soils lie under sediment or volcanic ash, in steep cliffs beneath younger soils, or where younger soil has eroded away, as in the Badlands of South Dakota.
Buried soils lose their vegetation and organic matter, but the shape and size of root traces still reveal the kind of vegetation they carried.
Chemical analysis centres on lime content, but X-ray diffraction, developed since the 1960s, now lets paleosols be placed in the 12 soil orders.
Many Precambrian soils fit no modern order and are grouped as 'green clays', coloured by unoxidized minerals that formed before free oxygen.
It sheds light on ancient ecosystems and on how life moved onto land in the Paleozoic, and it feeds the emerging field of astropedology.

definition.text: The moisture, temperature and other climatic conditions within a soil's pores, a special kind of microclimate.

facts.text: In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate; in waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere.
Classifying soils by climate data has been challenged by classifying them on observable features; the WRB counts soil climate only as a soil-forming factor.
Climate-sensitive soil features allow a broad reading of past climate from paleosols, though soils record climate less precisely than instruments.
Estimates of soil climate are now entering soil classification, models of soil formation and soil biology.

definition.text: Footprints, burrows, coprolites and root traces preserved in fossil soils as evidence of the activity of past organisms.

facts.text: Trace fossils rarely identify a species, but unlike body fossils they usually stay where the organism lived, so they record its behaviour, as with the shallow burrows of solitary bees.
Root-trace patterns and horizon sequences reveal the plant formation, such as forest, woodland or grassland, even when the species cannot be named.
Paleosols can themselves be seen as trace fossils of whole ancient ecosystems.

definition.text: Estimating the vanished parent material of a fossil soil from nearby materials, to measure how much soil formation took place.

facts.text: Soils start much like their parent material and lose its features over time, so a baseline is needed to judge how far formation went.
Comparing soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, or lithosequences, shows what role the parent material played.
Estimates rest on four assumptions: the proxy material is fresh, it was uniform through the profile, at least one constituent survived weathering, and volume change tracks thickness and density.
No constituent is fully immune to weathering: quartz is fairly stable above pH 9, alumina between pH 4.5 and 8, and lead and zirconium over wider ranges.

definition.text: The fossil record of soils, made up chiefly of paleosols buried by flood sediments or volcanic deposits, or preserved at geological unconformities.

facts.text: After burial, organic matter decays, iron oxidizes from Fe2+ to Fe3+ and hydrous ferric oxides dry out, which makes fossil soils harder to recognize.
Telltale signs are downward-branching root traces, gradual alteration below a sharp former land surface, and crack patterns like peds and cutans.
Most fossil soils fit the twelve USDA orders, usually identified by X-ray diffraction; only some very old soils with a grey-green horizon formed without oxygen do not.
With little or no ozone layer, Precambrian soils eroded fast, and most are undeveloped Entisols or Inceptisols; Vertisols and Aridisols run continuously from the Paleoproterozoic.
Outside ice ages Oxisols have dominated the record, because new soil formation needs the glaciation and mountain building that come with cooler times.
Land plants brought new orders: Histosols in the Devonian, Alfisols and Ultisols in the late Devonian and early Carboniferous, while Mollisols spread only from the Miocene as grasslands evolved.
Gelisol fossils are confined to times of extensive continental glaciation, the earliest 900 million years ago in the Neoproterozoic.
Unlike fossil plants and animals, very few fossil soils are of extinct types, which makes them useful for reading past ecosystems.

title: Soil in the United States

definition.text: The varied soils of the United States, classified in USDA soil taxonomy down to the series, each a unique kind of soil.

facts.text: Over 20,000 soil series have been identified, and soil maps cover more than 95 percent of U.S. counties, served online through Web Soil Survey.
Estimated shares of U.S. land, territories included, put Mollisols first at 21.5%, then Alfisols (14%), Entisols (12.3%), Inceptisols (9.7%) and Ultisols (9.2%); Oxisols cover 0.02%.
Mollisols lie mostly on the Great Plains, Aridisols in the dry West, Gelisols only in Alaska, Ultisols in warm humid regions, and Spodosols under cool conifer forest and in Florida.
Federal authority for U.S. soil survey dates from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896; today the National Cooperative Soil Survey, led by the NRCS, carries it out.

conflicts.text: USDA soil taxonomy says more than 14,000 soil series are recognised in the United States.
conflicts.note: Soil in the United States (S:2b19c920025c) says over 20,000; both are lower bounds, probably from different dates.

notes: The composition table covers the US with associated territories, so its shares (Mollisols 21.5%, Gelisols 8.7%) differ slightly from the U.S. ice-free-land shares in USDA soil taxonomy#Soil Orders (22.4%, 7.5%); different scope, not a conflict.

definition.text: A suborder of Inceptisols in USDA soil taxonomy for soils showing evidence of human habitation and farming.

facts.text: Anthrepts have a plaggen or anthropic epipedon, a sign of intense and prolonged human activity.

definition.text: A suborder of Aridisols in USDA soil taxonomy that has accumulated high levels of residual or dust-fall calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Calcids have a calcic, hypercalcic or petrocalcic horizon whose top lies within 1.0 m of the surface.
Their parent materials are rich in carbonate or received it as dust, and rainfall has been too low to remove it or move it deep.
Most are rangeland or wildlife habitat, some irrigated cropland, where micronutrient deficiency is normal.
Great groups include Salicalcids, Gypsicalcids, Petrocalcids, Hypercalcids and Haplocalcids.

definition.text: The five suborders of Ultisols in USDA soil taxonomy, set by wetness, organic matter and climate.

facts.text: Aquults have a water table at or near the surface for much of the year; Udults are Ultisols of humid climates.
Ustults are Ultisols of semiarid and subhumid climates; Xerults are temperate ones with arid summers and moist winters.
Humults are well-drained and rich in organic matter, which makes them relatively fertile, as in the Olympic series.
Great groups build on the suborder name: the Cecil series is Typic Kanhapludults, the Bama series Typic Paleudults.
